answer.label: Not Thomas Jefferson — no such letter has ever been produced
answer.authorDates: Unattributed · no manuscript or printed letter located
answer.sourceLine: Wikiquote files this under Disputed. Its only citation there is John E. Remsburg’s Six Historic Americans (1906), which attributes it to a Jefferson letter addressed to a ‘Dr. Woods’ — a letter Remsburg does not reproduce, and which Wikiquote notes has never been reproduced since. Wikiquote also reports that the Thomas Jefferson Foundation, which maintains Monticello, lists the quotation as spurious.

source.excerpt: I have recently been examining all the known superstitions of the world, and do not find in our particular superstition one redeeming feature. They are all alike founded on fables and mythology.
trail: Wikiquote’s Thomas Jefferson page ↗ places this line in its Disputed section — not in the sourced section — and gives its only citation as John E. Remsburg, Six Historic Americans (New York: The Truth Seeker Company, 1906), chapter 2, p. 74.

Wikiquote records two specific problems with that citation: Remsburg ‘claimed it to be from a letter to “Dr. Woods”’, and ‘the full letter is never reproduced’. An attributed letter that nobody has ever printed is the standard shape of a manufactured quotation.

The same Wikiquote entry reports that the Jefferson Foundation — the body that runs Monticello and maintains the standard reference list of spurious Jefferson quotations — lists this quotation as spurious. We were not able to read the Foundation’s page ourselves: monticello.org is unreachable from the environment this record was built in, so that finding is reported here at second hand, on Wikiquote’s authority, and not as something we confirmed at source.

We also could not read Remsburg’s 1906 text directly — archive.org, which hosts the scan Wikiquote links, was likewise unreachable, and Six Historic Americans is not on Wikisource or Project Gutenberg. The page and chapter given above are Wikiquote’s, not ours.
source.excerptNote: This is the fuller form as Wikiquote prints it. The second sentence is usually dropped in circulation, which is why the version people search for stops at ‘one redeeming feature’.
source.rightsNote: We are not asserting a rights status. Nobody has located an author or an original publication for this sentence, and a line whose origin is unknown is a line whose ownership is unknown. The 1906 book that carries Wikiquote’s only citation would itself be out of copyright in the United States, but that says nothing about where the words came from before Remsburg printed them.

author.name: Thomas Jefferson
author.heading: Why it gets pinned on Jefferson
author.metaLine: 1743–1826 · Third US president & author of the Declaration of Independence
author.bio: Thomas Jefferson drafted the Declaration of Independence, wrote the Virginia Statute for Religious Freedom, and served as the third president of the United States. He is one of the most heavily documented Americans of his century — his correspondence runs to tens of thousands of items — which is exactly what makes an unproduceable letter suspicious. He also wrote at length and sharply about organised religion, so a fabricated line in that register finds a ready audience. He died at Monticello on 4 July 1826.

misattribution.heading: Why this one does not stand up
misattribution.intro: Jefferson wrote a great deal about religion, and some of it is genuinely severe. That is precisely why a fabricated line in this register travels so easily — it sounds like him.

items.why: Remsburg’s 1906 book is the only source Wikiquote cites, and it notes that Remsburg ‘claimed it to be from a letter to “Dr. Woods”’ while ‘the full letter is never reproduced’. No manuscript, no recipient identified beyond a surname, no printed text read the Disputed entry ↗.

Wikiquote reports that the Jefferson Foundation lists the quotation as spurious. That is the body that maintains the reference list of Jefferson quotations, so its ruling is the one that matters — though we flag that we relied on Wikiquote for it rather than reading the Foundation’s page where we read it ↗.

Remsburg was an American freethought lecturer and writer, a president of the American Secular Union, and the author of polemics including The Christ (1909). A quotation that first surfaces inside a movement text arguing a case, with no document behind it, is evidence about the movement rather than about Jefferson his biography ↗.

items.who: Jefferson really did write about ‘monkish ignorance and superstition’
items.why: In his last letter, to Roger C. Weightman on 24 June 1826, Jefferson hoped the Declaration would be ‘the signal of arousing men to burst the chains under which monkish ignorance and superstition had persuaded them to bind themselves’. That is sourced, dated and in Wikiquote’s sourced section — and it is aimed at clerical authority, not at Christianity itself the genuine line ↗.

misattribution.truthLine: Nobody can say who wrote it. What can be said is that the only source ever offered is a 1906 book quoting a letter it does not print, and that the Jefferson Foundation calls the quotation spurious Wikiquote’s Disputed section ↗.

context.heading: The real Jefferson is stranger than the fake
lead: Jefferson’s actual writing on religion is not a blanket dismissal. He cut up copies of the Gospels to separate what he took to be the authentic moral teaching of Jesus from what he called the ‘fictions of his pseudo-followers’, and he defended that teaching as unsurpassed. He was scathing about priests and about doctrine; he was not scathing about Jesus.
The fabricated line collapses that distinction into a flat sneer, which is what makes it useful to whoever put it into circulation and useless as evidence about Jefferson.
context.pull: He was scathing about priests and about doctrine. He was not scathing about Jesus.
